Clinical Reference

Acute Kidney Injury

On this page
An abrupt (hours–days) drop in glomerular filtration — caught as a rising creatinine or a falling urine output — that is defined & staged by KDIGO and reversed by finding the insult: is the kidney under-perfused (prerenal), intrinsically injured (ATN / AIN / GN / vascular), or obstructed (postrenal)?
Prerenal · Intrinsic · Postrenal KDIGO stage 1–3 ~50% of ICU pts · stage 3 mortality >30% Restore perfusion · stop nephrotoxins
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

The glomerulus is a pressure filter. Filtration happens because the afferent arteriole (inflow) is held wide open while the efferent arteriole (outflow) is pinched — that pressure difference squeezes plasma across the membrane. Autoregulation keeps glomerular pressure (and GFR) nearly constant across a mean arterial pressure of roughly 80–180 mmHg using two levers: afferent dilation driven by prostaglandins & nitric oxide, and efferent constriction driven by angiotensin II.

Every cause of AKI is a failure of that machine, and they sort into three buckets. Prerenal = the kidney is structurally fine but starved of flow/pressure (hypovolemia, low cardiac output, sepsis vasodilation, hepatorenal). Intrinsic = the filter or tubules are damaged — ischemic/toxic acute tubular necrosis (ATN), allergic acute interstitial nephritis (AIN), glomerulonephritis (GN), or vascular. Postrenal = the drain is blocked (BPH, stones, malignancy, neurogenic bladder). Untreated prerenal ischemia is the commonest slide into ATN.

This is exactly why two drug classes cause “prerenal” AKI: NSAIDs block the afferent prostaglandins → the inflow tap constricts → glomerular pressure falls; ACE inhibitors / ARBs block angiotensin II at the efferent arteriole → the outflow relaxes → filtration pressure falls. Both are usually tolerated — until the patient is volume-depleted or renal-artery-dependent, when autoregulation was the only thing holding GFR up.

The nephron is a garden sprinkler. The afferent arteriole is the inflow hose; the efferent arteriole is the nozzle you thumb to build spray pressure. NSAIDs kink the hose (afferent constriction). ACEi/ARBs loosen the nozzle (efferent dilation). Either one drops the spray — the filtrate — even though the sprinkler itself is intact. Block the drain downstream (postrenal) and back-pressure eventually stops the whole thing.
Autoregulation holds GFR steady until volume/pressure fails or a drug removes a lever — then AKI, sorted into prerenal / intrinsic / postrenal.
The nephron: glomerulus → proximal tubule → loop of Henle → distal tubule → collecting duct. The proximal tubule & outer-medullary S3 segment are the most O₂-hungry and the first to die in ischemic ATN.
Piotr Michał Jaworski (PioM), Wikimedia Commons — KidneyStructures (CC BY-SA 3.0)
Gross anatomy: cortex, medullary pyramids, and the collecting system. Post-renal obstruction dilates the pelvicalyceal system (hydronephrosis); chronically small, echogenic kidneys signal CKD, not acute injury.
OpenStax College, Anatomy & Physiology — 2610 The Kidney (CC BY 3.0)
Read the whole guide through the three buckets: fluids fix prerenal flow, stopping the offending drug / steroids fix ATN & AIN, immunosuppression fixes GN, and a catheter or stent fixes postrenal. Dialysis buys time for any of them to recover — it treats the consequences (the AEIOU emergencies), never the cause.
🔬

ATN, and the other intrinsic injuries — what actually breaks

Ischemic/toxic ATN is the commonest intrinsic AKI in the hospital. Tubular epithelial cells lose their polarity, shed their apical brush border into the lumen (→ muddy-brown granular casts), and detach — which (1) obstructs the tubule, (2) lets filtrate back-leak across the denuded epithelium, and (3) triggers tubuloglomerular feedback afferent vasoconstriction. GFR falls out of proportion to the histology. Because tubular cells can regenerate, ATN is usually reversible over 1–3 weeks if the insult stops — often through a polyuric recovery phase.

Intrinsic patternTriggerMechanism (why the filter fails)
Ischemic ATNProlonged prerenal, shock, sepsis, post-op hypotensionO₂ delivery to the S3 proximal & medullary thick ascending limb fails → ATP depletion → cell death, cast obstruction, backleak.
Toxic ATNAminoglycosides, vancomycin, amphotericin, cisplatin, IV contrast, myoglobin/hemoglobinDirect tubular toxicity + intrarenal vasoconstriction; pigment (rhabdo/hemolysis) also causes cast obstruction & oxidative injury.
AINPPIs, NSAIDs, β-lactams, sulfa, allopurinol; infection; autoimmuneCell-mediated hypersensitivity in the interstitium — eosinophils, sterile pyuria, WBC casts. Classic (rare) triad: rash, fever, eosinophilia. Treat by stopping the drug ± steroids.
GN / vasculitisAnti-GBM, ANCA, lupus, IgA, post-infectiousImmune injury to the glomerular capillary → hematuria, RBC casts, proteinuria, hypertension. A nephrology emergency (RPGN) — biopsy & immunosuppress.
VascularTTP/HUS, scleroderma renal crisis, atheroemboli, renal artery/vein occlusionMicrovascular thrombosis or large-vessel occlusion cuts perfusion at the vessel level; look for schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, LDH.
ATN histology: flattened, necrotic tubular epithelium with luminal debris and loss of the brush border — the microscopic correlate of muddy-brown casts.
Amadalvarez, Wikimedia Commons — Necrosi tubular aguda renal (CC BY-SA 4.0)
Dark, “tea-colored” urine of rhabdomyolysis: myoglobin dips heme-positive on the urine strip but shows no RBCs on microscopy — a heme-positive/RBC-negative mismatch that flags pigment nephropathy. Check a CK.
James Heilman, MD, Wikimedia Commons — RhabdoUrine (CC BY-SA 3.0)

Presentation, imaging & labs — and why

🩺

Symptoms & signs — frequency and the mechanism behind each

The most important point about AKI presentation: it is usually clinically silent and found on labs. A rising creatinine or a quiet drop in urine output is the presentation — symptoms appear only with volume overload, uremia, or the underlying cause. Frequencies below are approximate and refer to symptomatic AKI; oliguria is present in only ~50–60% (non-oliguric ATN is common and carries a better prognosis).

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Rising creatinine / BUN (detected on labs)~100%Definitional — falling GFR reduces clearance of creatinine (a muscle metabolite) and urea. Often the only finding.
Oliguria (UOP <400–500 mL/day)~50–60%Reduced filtrate + avid tubular Na⁺/water reabsorption (prerenal) or tubular obstruction/backleak (ATN). Absent in non-oliguric ATN.
Fatigue, malaise, anorexia~40–60%Accumulating uremic solutes depress appetite and energy; often the first thing the patient notices.
Volume overload (edema, dyspnea, ↑BP, crackles)~25–40%Kidney can’t excrete Na⁺/water → expanded ECF; worse with continued IV fluids or in HF/CKD.
Nausea / vomiting~20–35%Uremic gastropathy and metabolic acidosis stimulate the chemoreceptor trigger zone.
Tea/cola-colored or foamy urine<15%Cola-colored = glomerular hematuria or pigment (rhabdo/hemolysis); frothy = heavy proteinuria — both point intrinsic.
Flank pain / palpable bladder<15%Obstruction: stones/clot stretch the ureter; a distended bladder = outlet obstruction (BPH, neurogenic) — a bedside catheter is diagnostic and therapeutic.
Uremic encephalopathy, asterixis, pericardial friction rub<10%Severe/late uremia — an emergency indication for dialysis. Pericardial rub warns of uremic pericarditis (risk of tamponade).
Read the patternSilent ↑Cr + bland urine + a clear prerenal story (vomiting, diuretics, sepsis) → prerenal. ↑Cr + muddy-brown casts + a shock/toxin exposure → ATN. ↑Cr + hematuria/RBC casts/proteinuria/HTN → GN — call nephrology today. ↑Cr + distended bladder / hydronephrosis → postrenal — decompress now.
🪛

Imaging — what a renal ultrasound tells you, and when to order it

FindingWhen it mattersWhat it means
Hydronephrosis / dilated collecting systemRule out first in unexplained AKIPostrenal obstruction until proven otherwise. Bilateral (or unilateral in a single kidney) is the surgically reversible cause you never want to miss.
Small (<9 cm), echogenic kidneys, thin cortexDistinguish acute vs chronicChronic kidney disease — not acute injury. Changes management & prognosis (may reflect irreversible baseline).
Normal-to-enlarged kidneys, increased echogenicityIntrinsic AKIConsistent with acute medical renal disease (ATN, AIN, GN, infiltration).
Elevated resistive index (Doppler >0.7)AdjunctNonspecific; very high RI can suggest intrinsic/ATN over prerenal, and screens for renal vein/artery flow.
Absent arterial/venous flowSuspected vascularRenal artery thrombus/dissection or renal vein thrombosis — rare but time-critical.
Marked hydronephrosis with cortical thinning — dilated, fluid-filled calyces ballooning the collecting system. The picture of postrenal obstruction; relieve it before the pressure destroys nephrons.
Hansen & Nielsen et al., Wikimedia Commons — End-stage hydronephrosis (CC BY 4.0)
Normal renal Doppler with resistive-index waveform. US needs no contrast and no iodine load — the safe first imaging test in AKI.
Hansen & Nielsen et al., Wikimedia Commons — Renal Doppler RI (CC BY 4.0)
Order a renal ultrasound when AKI is unexplained, not improving in 24–48 h, or obstruction is possible (single kidney, pelvic malignancy, BPH, anticholinergics, stone history). You do not need one for every obvious prerenal case that corrects with fluids — but a low threshold is correct because obstruction is silent and fully reversible if caught early.
🧪

Reading the labs — what each value is telling you (and what fakes it)

LabWhat it means & why it moves — confounders
CreatinineFiltered marker of GFR, but it lags real-time GFR by 24–72 h and is buffered by tubular secretion — so early AKI is under-called. Falsely high without true GFR change: trimethoprim, cimetidine, cobicistat, dolutegravir (block tubular secretion); high muscle mass; ketoacidosis (assay interference). Falsely low (masking AKI): low muscle mass, cachexia, cirrhosis, amputation, dilution from fluids. A “normal” Cr in a frail elder can hide a halved GFR.
BUN & BUN:Cr ratioUrea is filtered and reabsorbed with Na⁺/water, so avid prerenal reabsorption raises BUN out of proportion → ratio >20:1 suggests prerenal. Falsely high BUN: GI bleed (protein load), steroids, catabolism, high-protein feeds, tetracyclines. Falsely low: liver failure (↓urea synthesis), low protein intake, over-hydration — which mutes the ratio.
FENa = (Uₙₐ×P_Cr)/(Pₙₐ×U_Cr)×100<1% → prerenal (avid Na⁺ retention); >2% → ATN (tubules can’t reabsorb Na⁺). Invalid on diuretics (falsely high — use FEUrea instead), and falsely low in contrast/pigment nephropathy, early GN, HRS, and any prerenal-on-CKD state.
FEUrea = (U_urea×P_Cr)/(BUN×U_Cr)×100<35% → prerenal. Because urea handling is less diuretic-sensitive, FEUrea stays useful after loop diuretics, where FENa fails.
PotassiumRises because the failing kidney can’t excrete the daily K⁺ load; worsened by acidosis (K⁺ shifts out of cells), tissue breakdown (rhabdo, tumor lysis, hemolysis), and RAASi/K-sparing drugs. The value that most often forces emergent action.
Bicarbonate / anion gapHigh-anion-gap metabolic acidosis from retained organic/uremic acids (and lactate if hypoperfused). Severe acidemia (pH <7.1) is an RRT trigger.
Phosphate, calcium, uric acidPhosphate and uric acid rise (↓excretion; released in tumor lysis/rhabdo); calcium often falls (binds phosphate, ↓calcitriol). The Ca↓/PO₄↑/K↑/uric-acid↑ quartet is the fingerprint of tumor lysis and crush injury.
CKRhabdomyolysis risk rises sharply once CK >5,000 U/L (esp. >15,000–40,000); a heme-positive dipstick with no RBCs on micro should trigger a CK.
Urine microscopyThe cheapest, highest-yield test: muddy-brown granular casts = ATN; WBC casts / eosinophils = AIN; dysmorphic RBCs & RBC casts = GN; bland sediment = prerenal or postrenal; crystals = crystalline nephropathy.
Formed elements of urine sediment. Casts are tubular casts of protein & cells — the shape (granular vs cellular vs RBC vs WBC) localizes the injury within the nephron.
Lehmann R., Wikimedia Commons — Formed elements of urine (CC BY 4.0)
Granular casts on microscopy. Coarse, pigmented (“muddy-brown”) granular casts are the hallmark of established ATN; RBC casts instead point to glomerulonephritis.
Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya, Wikimedia Commons — Granular casts (CC BY 4.0)

Classification at a glance — prerenal vs ATN vs postrenal

ParameterPrerenalIntrinsic ATNPostrenal (early)
BUN:Cr>20:110–15:1Variable
FENa<1%>2%Variable (>1% if prolonged)
FEUrea<35%>50%Variable
Urine Na⁺<20 mEq/L>40 mEq/LVariable
Urine osmolality>500 mOsm/kg (concentrated)<350 (isosthenuric, ~300)<350
Urine sedimentBland / hyaline castsMuddy-brown granular castsBland ± crystals/RBC
Response to fluidsCr improvesNo quick improvementImproves after decompression
Caveats that trip people upFENa <1% is not unique to prerenal — it’s also low in contrast nephropathy, pigment (rhabdo/hemolysis), early GN, and hepatorenal syndrome, because all cause intense renal vasoconstriction. And FENa is uninterpretable after a loop diuretic — switch to FEUrea <35% there.
The three-bucket workup: exclude obstruction, read the urine, then match therapy to the cause — and dialyze urgently only for an AEIOU emergency.

Assess

Recognizing AKI in clinic

🔍

How outpatient AKI shows up

In clinic, AKI is almost always a lab surprise: a creatinine that jumped since the last BMP, often in a patient who feels well. Your job is to (1) confirm it fits the KDIGO definition against a real baseline, (2) sort it into a bucket, and (3) decide who can be worked up as an outpatient vs sent in.

Who is at risk (and who tips over with a small insult): CKD, diabetes, heart failure, cirrhosis, age >65, solitary kidney, and anyone on the “triple whammy” (NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic). The classic trigger is a dehydrating illness — vomiting, diarrhea, poor intake, or a new diuretic dose — layered on top of that physiology.

Always anchor to a baseline creatinine: the lowest stable value in the last 7–365 days. Without one, a “normal-looking” 1.4 mg/dL may be a doubling from 0.7. If no prior value exists, KDIGO back-calculates an assumed baseline from eGFR 75 — but that overestimates AKI in occult CKD, so interpret cautiously.

KDIGO AKI stage calculator

Stage = the worse of the creatinine criterion or the urine-output criterion. Enter what you have.

≥0.5 mL/kg/h (adequate)
<0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 h
<0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥12 h
<0.3 mL/kg/h ≥24 h or anuria ≥12 h
—

Also stage 3 automatically if SCr ≥4.0 mg/dL (with acute rise) or RRT is started. Source: KDIGO 2012 AKI, Table 2.

🧪

Labs & imaging — the bucket-sorting workup

Treat

Outpatient management

💊

Stepwise — remove the insult, protect the kidney

There is no drug that “treats AKI.” The therapy is to restore perfusion, remove nephrotoxins, and relieve obstruction — everything below is a version of one of those three moves, matched to the bucket.
1
First-line — stop the offenders & fix volume
Nephrotoxin stewardship + the “sick-day” medication holds.
▾

Hold on sick days (mnemonic “SAD-MANS”): Sulfonylureas, ACEi, Diuretics, Metformin, ARBs, NSAIDs, SGLT2 inhibitors — during any acute dehydrating illness. Stop NSAIDs outright; defer elective contrast.

Drug / classStart / what to doTarget / when to resumeWhy it worksIf allergic / alternative
NSAIDsStopAvoid in CKD/at-risk; use scheduled acetaminophenRestores afferent prostaglandin dilation → recovers glomerular inflow pressureAcetaminophen; topical NSAID (low systemic); short opioid course if severe
ACEi / ARBHold during acute AKI/illnessRestart when SCr stable & K⁺ normal; tolerate ≤30% baseline SCr rise on chronic therapyRemoving efferent blockade restores filtration pressure acutely; long-term they are renoprotective in proteinuric CKDIf ACEi cough → ARB; if both intolerant → amlodipine / other agent for BP
SGLT2 inhibitorHold on sick days / acute AKIResume when eating/drinking & stable; expect a small reversible eGFR dip that is NOT AKIAvoids volume depletion & euglycemic DKA during illness; long-term renoprotective (dapa-/empagliflozin)Continue other glucose-lowering (insulin) during the hold
MetforminHold if AKI or eGFR <30, and around iodinated contrast in higher-risk patientsResume 48 h post-contrast once SCr confirmed stableRenal clearance falls in AKI → accumulation → lactic acidosis riskInsulin, DPP-4 inhibitor (renally dosed), or GLP-1 RA during the hold
Loop diureticReduce/hold if volume-deplete (prerenal); continue only for true overloadRe-dose to euvolemiaOver-diuresis is itself a prerenal insult; it does not prevent or treat ATNSee ward diuretic table for loop-to-loop swaps & sulfa alternatives
2
Treat the bucket
Match therapy to prerenal / intrinsic / postrenal.
▾
  • Prerenal: gentle oral or IV rehydration if truly hypovolemic; treat the driver (GI losses, HF decongestion, sepsis). Reassess — don’t fluid-load a euvolemic or overloaded patient.
  • AIN (drug): stop the culprit (PPI, NSAID, antibiotic, allopurinol); many recover on withdrawal alone. Persistent/severe → nephrology ± corticosteroids.
  • GN / vasculitis: urgent nephrology — this is not an outpatient wait-and-see; RPGN needs biopsy and immunosuppression to save nephrons.
  • Postrenal: bladder scan; a Foley relieves outlet obstruction immediately; upper-tract obstruction → urology/IR for stent or nephrostomy.
3
Refer nephrology
When outpatient management isn’t enough.
▾

Refer for: rapidly rising creatinine, KDIGO stage 3 or eGFR <30, glomerular findings (hematuria/RBC casts/heavy proteinuria), AKI without a clear cause, recurrent AKI, or suspected systemic disease. Send in urgently (ED) rather than refer if any red flag below is present.

Cockcroft–Gault creatinine clearance (drug dosing)

CrCl = [(140−age) × weight(kg) × (0.85 if female)] / (72 × SCr). The estimate most drug labels use for renal dose adjustment.

Male
Female (×0.85)
—

Caution: unreliable in unstable/rapidly changing SCr, extremes of body weight, and low muscle mass. For staging AKI use the KDIGO calculator, not eGFR.

Monitor

Follow-up cadence

📈

What to recheck, and when

  • After an AKI event: recheck BMP in 3–7 days (sooner if stage 2–3 or symptomatic); confirm the creatinine is trending back toward baseline.
  • After restarting ACEi/ARB or up-titrating a diuretic: BMP in 1–2 weeks — watch K⁺ and SCr (accept ≤30% SCr rise).
  • After a full episode: AKI predicts future CKD — recheck kidney function & urine albumin at ~3 months to define the new baseline (AKD → CKD boundary).
  • Reconcile the med list every visit for re-introduced nephrotoxins; counsel on sick-day rules.
Prevent

USPSTF A/B & prevention

🛡️

What actually has a Grade A/B — and what doesn’t

Honesty noteThe USPSTF has no recommendation to screen asymptomatic adults for AKI or CKD — the general-population kidney-screening question is an I-statement (insufficient evidence). Risk-based kidney testing (in diabetes, HTN, CVD) is KDIGO/expert-guided, not USPSTF-graded. So the highest-value “prevention” of AKI is controlling the diseases that damage kidneys — and those do have Grade A/B statements:
GradeRecommendationPopulation / relevance to kidney risk
AScreen for hypertension (office BP, confirmed out-of-office)Adults ≥18 — HTN is a leading driver of CKD and a modifier of AKI risk
BScreen for prediabetes & type 2 diabetesAdults 35–70 with overweight/obesity — diabetes is the top cause of CKD
BStatin for primary prevention of CVDAdults 40–75 with ≥1 risk factor & 10-yr risk ≥10% — shared cardiorenal risk
ATobacco cessation counseling + pharmacotherapyAll adults — smoking accelerates renal & vascular disease
BIntensive behavioral counseling for obesityBMI ≥30 — obesity-related glomerulopathy & diabetes risk

Vaccinate CKD/at-risk patients (influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal, hepatitis B) — infection precipitates AKI. The most direct AKI prevention is nephrotoxin avoidance and periprocedural hydration.

Escalate

When to refer / admit

🚑

Red flags → ED / admission

Send in — not “recheck next week” — for any of: K⁺ >6.0 mEq/L or any hyperkalemic ECG change; volume overload / pulmonary edema; severe metabolic acidosis (HCO₃⁻ <15 or pH <7.2); uremic symptoms (encephalopathy, pericardial rub, unexplained nausea); oligo-/anuria; rapidly rising creatinine; suspected obstruction needing decompression; or glomerular features (RBC casts, hematuria + proteinuria + HTN) suggesting RPGN.
Hyperkalemia with ECG changes (peaked T waves → widened QRS → sine wave) is a cardiac-arrest risk. Give IV calcium immediately and transfer — see the Wards hyperkalemia module.
🛏️ Wards — inpatient AKI: fluids, potassium, decongestion & daily trends
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria & initial profile

Admit for KDIGO stage 2–3, or any complication that can’t be safely managed at home:

  • Hyperkalemia (K⁺ >6 or ECG changes), refractory metabolic acidosis, or symptomatic uremia
  • Volume overload / pulmonary edema requiring IV diuresis or monitoring
  • Oligo-/anuria, rapidly rising creatinine, or need for urgent workup (possible RPGN, myeloma, TMA)
  • Obstruction requiring urology/IR intervention
  • The precipitant itself needs admission (sepsis, GI bleed, decompensated HF/cirrhosis)
First bedside question on admission: volume status. Hypovolemic → resuscitate. Overloaded → decongest. Obstructed → catheter/US. Get this right before ordering anything else.

Treat

Acute management

💊

Stepwise inpatient therapy

1
Restore perfusion — balanced crystalloids
If hypovolemic/prerenal. Reassess responsiveness, don’t auto-bolus.
▾
Fluids fix the prerenal bucket by restoring renal blood flow before ischemia becomes ATN. Once ATN is established, more fluid only causes overload — so titrate to response, not to a fixed number.

Choose a balanced crystalloid (Lactated Ringer’s / Plasma-Lyte) over 0.9% saline for most resuscitation to avoid hyperchloremic acidosis. SMART & SALT-ED showed a lower composite of death/RRT/renal dysfunction with balanced fluids; BaSICS and PLUS found no mortality difference — net: balanced is at least as safe and a reasonable default; avoid large-volume saline.

Dose: 500 mL–1 L bolus of LR/Plasma-Lyte, then reassess (BP, UOP, exam, passive-leg-raise/POCUS). Repeat only if fluid-responsive. LR is safe in hyperkalemia (its 4 mEq/L K⁺ is negligible and it corrects acidosis).

2
Treat hyperkalemia — the cocktail
Stabilize → shift → remove. See the dedicated table below.
▾

If K⁺ ≥6.0 (or any ECG change): calcium first to protect the heart, then insulin+glucose ± albuterol to shift, then a binder ± loop diuretic (or dialysis) to remove. Full doses in the hyperkalemia module.

3
Decongest / correct acidosis / remove toxins
Loop diuretics for overload; bicarb for severe acidemia.
▾
  • Volume overload: IV loop diuretic (dose table below); if resistant → continuous infusion or sequential nephron blockade (add thiazide/metolazone). Diuretics do not prevent/treat ATN — they only manage volume.
  • Metabolic acidosis: treat the cause; isotonic sodium bicarbonate for pH <7.1–7.2 or as a bridge to RRT.
  • Nephrotoxins: remove; AUC-guide vancomycin (400–600 mg·h/L); once-daily aminoglycosides with levels or avoid.

Hyperkalemia — the emergency cocktail (doses)

Use calcium chloride 10% 5–10 mL via central line if peri-arrest (3× elemental Ca)

AgentStartTitration → maxWhy / when to pick itIf allergic / alternative

Metolazone (add-on)PO 2.5–5 mg, 30 min before the loopUp to 10 mg/daySequential nephron blockade for loop resistance — blocks distal Na⁺ reabsorption the loop can’t reachChlorothiazide 500 mg IV if no enteral route; watch K⁺/Mg⁺ wasting
Furosemide Stress Test: give 1.0 mg/kg IV (loop-naïve) or 1.5 mg/kg IV (prior loop exposure). If urine output is <200 mL over the next 2 h, the patient is likely to progress to stage 3 AKI / need RRT (≈87% sensitivity, 84% specificity) — a functional stress test of tubular reserve, not a treatment.
What does NOT help“Renal-dose” dopamine, mannitol, and loop diuretics given to prevent or reverse ATN are ineffective and can harm — KDIGO recommends against them. Diuretics are for volume management only.
Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend each day

  • SCr & BUN — rising, plateaued, or recovering? Recovery often passes through a polyuric phase — replace losses and watch K⁺/Mg⁺/Phos.
  • K⁺, HCO₃⁻, Ca, Phos, Mg — the electrolyte quartet that forces escalation.
  • Strict I/O + daily weight — the single best guide to fluid decisions.
  • Urine output trend — the earliest signal of recovery or worsening.
  • Volume exam — JVP, edema, lung exam; re-decide fluids vs diuresis each morning.
  • Med list — re-check renal dosing as GFR changes; hold anything newly nephrotoxic.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers

Transfer to ICU / call nephrology for urgent RRT when: refractory hyperkalemia (persistent K⁺ ≥6.5 despite the cocktail); severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.1) not correcting; pulmonary edema needing NIV or intubation; hemodynamic instability requiring vasopressors; symptomatic uremia (encephalopathy, pericarditis, bleeding); a dialyzable intoxication; or an FST-predicted rapid progression with worsening oligo-anuria.
The AEIOU emergencies (Acidosis, Electrolytes, Intoxication, Overload, Uremia) are the only indications to dialyze urgently — outside them, the trials favor watchful waiting (see ICU panel).
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: creatinine plateaued or improving toward baseline; K⁺, HCO₃⁻ and volume controlled off IV therapy; precipitant treated; nephrotoxins reconciled with a clear restart plan for ACEi/ARB/SGLT2i/metformin; and outpatient BMP follow-up arranged in 3–7 days.

Home

Recovering AKI, stable electrolytes/volume, reliable follow-up & med access.

Home health

Home + nursing for labs/IV or teaching (e.g., new diuretic regimen, weights).

SNF

Needs 24 h skilled nursing (frequent labs, deconditioning) but <3 h therapy/day.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Recovered enough to tolerate ≥3 h therapy/day (e.g., post-critical-illness weakness).

LTAC

Prolonged complex needs — e.g., continued dialysis + vent weaning after prolonged ICU stay.

Outpatient dialysis / hospice

Dialysis-dependent → arrange chronic access & a unit slot; hospice if goals are comfort-focused (e.g., dialysis declined in advanced illness).
Every AKI survivor needs a documented AKI diagnosis, a med-restart plan, and nephrology/PCP follow-up — AKI roughly doubles long-term CKD and mortality risk, and the biggest failure mode is nephrotoxins silently restarted without a recheck.
🫀 ICU — RRT timing, CRRT, shock/hepatorenal & downgrade
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When AKI belongs in the unit — AEIOU

The emergent RRT indications double as ICU triggers — remember AEIOU:

LetterIndicationThreshold / example
AcidosisSevere metabolic acidosis refractory to therapypH <7.1 not correcting with bicarbonate
ElectrolytesRefractory hyperkalemia (or other severe derangement)K⁺ ≥6.5 despite the medical cocktail
IntoxicationDialyzable toxinMethanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate, lithium, valproate, metformin/lactate
OverloadDiuretic-refractory volume overloadPulmonary edema not responding to high-dose loops
UremiaSymptomatic uremiaEncephalopathy, pericarditis (rub), uremic bleeding

Also admit for shock-associated AKI needing vasopressors, or any patient in whom you anticipate needing CRRT.

Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Dialysis catheter (temporary non-tunneled, ideally right IJ) if RRT is likely; arterial line for continuous MAP in shock; central line for pressors.
  • Hourly urine output (Foley), strict I/O, daily weight; frequent VBG for pH/K⁺; ionized calcium if on citrate CRRT.
  • Targets: MAP ≥65 mmHg, avoid both hypoperfusion and iatrogenic fluid overload (both worsen renal outcomes), K⁺ and pH corrected.
Support

RRT, pressors & hepatorenal

💉

Renal replacement — timing, modality, dose

The timing verdict: outside an AEIOU emergency, early/accelerated RRT does not improve survival — and increases dialysis dependence and line complications. Watchful waiting is preferred. STARRT-AKI, AKIKI, IDEAL-ICU and AKIKI 2 are concordant; ELAIN (single-center, surgical) is the lone positive outlier.
  • Modality: CRRT for hemodynamically unstable patients and acute brain injury/↑ICP (gentler on hemodynamics & osmolality); intermittent HD when stable or for rapid solute removal (e.g., severe hyperkalemia, some intoxications). They are complementary.
  • Dose: CRRT effluent 20–25 mL/kg/h (prescribe ~25 to cover downtime); IHD Kt/V ~3.9/week. Higher intensity gives no survival benefit (RENAL 40 vs 25; ATN intensive vs standard).
  • Anticoagulation: regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) is first-line for CRRT (longer circuit life, less bleeding) unless contraindicated (severe liver failure/shock with citrate accumulation) — KDIGO; supported by RICH.
Extracorporeal blood-purification circuit. In the ICU, continuous therapy (CVVH/CVVHD/CVVHDF) removes fluid and solute slowly enough for the unstable patient to tolerate.
Jackhsiao, Wikimedia Commons — Hemodialysis machine (Public domain)
Hyperkalemia ECG: tall, tented (“peaked”) T waves — the earliest change, progressing to PR prolongation, QRS widening, and a sine wave. An ECG red alert that demands immediate IV calcium.
Jer5150, Wikimedia Commons — Hyperkalemia ECG (CC BY-SA 3.0)

Vasopressors & vasoconstrictors in AKI-associated shock / HRS

AgentReceptors / mechanismDoseEffectWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα₁ > β₁0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min (titrate)↑SVR, mild ↑CO → restores renal perfusion pressureFirst-line for septic/distributive shock; target MAP ≥65
VasopressinV₁ receptor (non-adrenergic)0.03 units/min (fixed add-on)↑SVR, catecholamine-sparing; efferent vasoconstriction may aid GFRAdd-on when norepinephrine dose is climbing
TerlipressinV₁ agonist (splanchnic vasoconstriction)1 mg IV q6h → 2 mg q6h by day 3 if SCr not ↓; or 2 mg/day continuous↑effective arterial volume → reverses HRS-AKI physiologyHRS-AKI (with albumin) — see below
Epinephrineβ₁ = β₂ > α₁0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑CO & ↑SVR; ↑lactateSecond/third-line; refractory shock
Angiotensin IIAT₁ receptorStart 20 ng/kg/min, titratePotent ↑SVR; efferent constrictionCatecholamine-refractory vasodilatory shock (esp. with AKI on RRT — ATHOS-3 subgroup)
The renal goal of every pressor here is the same: raise renal perfusion pressure (MAP − renal venous pressure). That means both defending MAP (α-agonism) and relieving venous congestion — a pressor plus decongestion often beats either alone.

Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS-AKI)

Diagnosis: AKI in cirrhosis with ascites, no improvement after ≥2 days off diuretics + albumin 1 g/kg/day (max 100 g), no shock, no nephrotoxins, and no structural injury (bland urine, no significant proteinuria/hematuria, normal US).

  • Terlipressin 1 mg IV q6h (or 2 mg/24 h continuous), up-titrate to 2 mg q6h if SCr not falling by day 3, plus albumin ~1 g/kg day 1 then 20–40 g/day. CONFIRM showed higher HRS reversal (32% vs 17%) but more respiratory failure — avoid in ACLF-3/hypoxemia.
  • ICU alternative: norepinephrine 0.5–3 mg/h + albumin (titrate MAP up ~10 mmHg). Non-ICU (US): midodrine 7.5–12.5 mg PO TID + octreotide 100–200 mcg SC TID + albumin.
  • Definitive: liver transplant.

Contrast-associated AKI & rhabdomyolysis

  • Contrast-AKI prevention: IV isotonic saline hydration + minimize contrast volume. PRESERVE: no benefit of sodium bicarbonate over saline and no benefit of NAC — don’t use them. SCr peaks day 3–5, usually recovers by 7–10 days.
  • Rhabdomyolysis: aggressive isotonic crystalloid early, titrated to urine output 200–300 mL/h; watch for overload & the K↑/PO₄↑/Ca↓ triad. Urinary alkalinization/mannitol are unproven — don’t let them delay volume. CK >5,000 flags risk.
Airway

Volume overload & respiratory support

🌬️

Cardiorenal pulmonary edema — NIV vs RRT for the lungs

Diuretic-refractory pulmonary edema from oligo-anuric AKI is an “O” (overload) indication for urgent RRT/ultrafiltration — dialysis is often the definitive way to offload the lungs when the kidneys won’t respond. Bridge oxygenation while you set up access:

First step
NIV (CPAP/BiPAP)
↓preload/afterload, recruits alveoli — buys time for UF
If intubated — mode
AC/VC
lung-protective
Tidal volume
6 mL/kg IBW
avoid volutrauma
PEEP
↑ to offload LV
titrate to oxygenation
If SpO₂ can’t be maintained on NIV, or the patient is tiring, intubate — then prioritize ultrafiltration/CRRT to remove the volume the kidneys can’t.
Rescue

Advanced / refractory options

⚙️

When the standard path stalls

  • Refractory vasodilatory shock with AKI: add vasopressin, then angiotensin II (ATHOS-3), high-dose/stress steroids for septic shock; treat source control aggressively.
  • Refractory hyperkalemia/overload: escalate from IHD to CRRT (or SLED) for continuous control; UF for pure fluid removal.
  • TMA (TTP/HUS, complement-mediated): urgent plasma exchange (TTP) or eculizumab (aHUS); hematology involvement.
  • Abdominal compartment syndrome: measure bladder pressure; decompress if >20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction — a reversible cause of olig-anuric AKI.
  • RPGN/vasculitis: pulse methylprednisolone + cyclophosphamide/rituximab ± plasma exchange (anti-GBM) — biopsy-guided, nephrology-led.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Step down when: hemodynamically stable off (or on minimal) vasopressors; K⁺, pH and volume corrected and stable; RRT either stopped (native UO returning, >400–500 mL/day off diuretics, SCr plateauing) or converted to a stable intermittent schedule deliverable on the floor; and no ongoing airway need.
Not yet if… the patient still needs continuous therapy (CRRT), pressors, or hourly titration; K⁺ or pH keeps rebounding; or urine output is falling again — those predict a bounce-back.

ICU disposition: dialysis-dependent survivors need chronic access + an outpatient unit; consider LTAC for prolonged combined organ support; and a frank goals-of-care conversation when AKI compounds advanced multi-organ failure (dialysis is not obligatory if it won’t meet the patient’s goals).

Interactions

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

🔗

How comorbidities change AKI — and what to hold

ComorbidityHow it changes the AKIHow it changes management
CKD (acute-on-chronic)Less reserve → faster hyperkalemia/acidosis; back-calculated baselines overstage; expect a permanent GFR step-down after severe AKINephrology early; renally dose everything; anticipate dialysis sooner; define new baseline at ~3 months
Heart failure (cardiorenal)Venous congestion drives AKI as much as low output; diuretic resistance commonDecongest rather than withhold diuretics; accept a modest SCr rise during effective decongestion; higher-dose/continuous loops ± thiazide; UF if refractory
CirrhosisHRS-AKI vs prerenal vs ATN overlap; splanchnic vasodilationAlbumin challenge (diagnostic + therapeutic); terlipressin/norepi for HRS; avoid over-diuresis & nephrotoxins; watch for SBP
DiabetesHigher CKD/AKI risk; contrast & drug sensitivityHold metformin (lactic acidosis) & SGLT2i (sick-day) during AKI; the SGLT2i eGFR dip is expected & renoprotective long-term
SepsisMost common ICU AKI; inflammatory + hemodynamic injuryBalanced fluids (avoid overload), early source control, norepinephrine to MAP ≥65; AUC-guided vancomycin
Drugs to avoid / use with caution in AKI: NSAIDs (avoid — afferent constriction & AIN); ACEi/ARB (hold during AKI, restart when stable); aminoglycosides (avoid/limit, once-daily + levels); vancomycin (AUC-guided 400–600 mg·h/L); iodinated contrast (minimize, saline-hydrate, no bicarb/NAC); metformin (hold if AKI or eGFR <30 / around contrast); SGLT2i (hold on sick days); gadolinium (avoid if eGFR <30 or any AKI — NSF risk); and renally dose DOACs, gabapentinoids, opioids, and antivirals.
Shared

Clinical pearls

💡

Sixteen numbers & rules that change management

Definition, memorized: AKI = ↑SCr ≥0.3 mg/dL in 48 h, or ↑SCr ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days, or UOP <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 h. Stage by the worse of the creatinine or urine-output column.
Anchor to a real baseline. A creatinine of 1.4 is stage 2 AKI if the baseline was 0.7 — and nothing if it was 1.3. Pull the old BMP before you act.
Creatinine lags. It takes 24–72 h to plateau, so early AKI is under-called and a falling creatinine still trails true recovery. Trend it; don’t treat a single value.
On diuretics, use FEUrea (<35% = prerenal), not FENa — loops make FENa falsely high. And remember FENa <1% is also seen in contrast, pigment, early GN, and HRS.
The “triple whammy” (NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic) is a top preventable prerenal cause. A ≤30% SCr rise after starting an ACEi/ARB is acceptable; >30% → look for renal-artery stenosis or over-diuresis.
Look at the urine yourself. Muddy-brown granular casts = ATN; WBC casts/eosinophils = AIN; RBC casts = GN; bland = prerenal/postrenal. The cheapest test with the highest yield.
Rule out obstruction early. A bladder scan and renal US catch a fully reversible cause that is otherwise silent — a Foley can be both diagnostic and therapeutic.
Early/accelerated RRT does not save lives (STARRT-AKI, AKIKI, IDEAL-ICU) and increases dialysis dependence — dialyze for AEIOU emergencies, otherwise watchful-wait.
CRRT effluent 20–25 mL/kg/h; more is not better (RENAL, ATN). Prefer regional citrate anticoagulation for the circuit (KDIGO).
Calcium first in hyperkalemia. It buys minutes but doesn’t lower K⁺ — insulin+glucose (± albuterol) does the shifting, and a binder or dialysis does the removing.
Loop equivalence: furosemide 40 mg IV = bumetanide 1 mg = torsemide 20 mg; oral furosemide is only ~50% bioavailable, so PO:IV = 2:1. True sulfa allergy → ethacrynic acid.
Furosemide stress test: 1.0 mg/kg (naïve) or 1.5 mg/kg (prior loops); UOP <200 mL over 2 h predicts progression to stage 3 / RRT.
Balanced crystalloids ≥ saline; avoid large-volume 0.9% saline (hyperchloremic acidosis). LR is safe in hyperkalemia — its 4 mEq/L K⁺ is trivial.
Contrast-AKI prevention = isotonic saline only. No bicarbonate, no NAC (PRESERVE). Minimize contrast volume; SCr peaks day 3–5.
HRS-AKI: terlipressin 1→2 mg IV q6h + albumin (1 g/kg day 1, then 20–40 g/day) reverses ~1/3 (CONFIRM) — watch for respiratory failure; norepinephrine + albumin is the ICU alternative.
AKI is not benign after discharge. It roughly doubles long-term CKD and death risk — document the diagnosis, write a nephrotoxin-restart plan, and recheck function at ~3 months to define the new baseline.

Sources, trials & credits

Guidelines & key references

  • KDIGO 2012 Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury (the current standing full guideline; definition, staging, RRT, dose) — kdigo.org (PDF). A formal update is in progress (Scope of Work, Oct 2023) — KDIGO AKI landing page.
  • KDOQI US Commentary on the KDIGO 2012 AKI Guideline (staging & baseline creatinine) — AJKD.
  • Acute Kidney Injury — StatPearls (classification, FENa/FEUrea, hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis) — NCBI Bookshelf.
  • Acute Kidney Injury — Merck Manual Professional (urine indices, microscopy, imaging) — merckmanuals.com.
  • ACR–NKF consensus on the use of iodinated contrast media in patients with kidney disease (2020) — Radiology.
  • 2020 ASHP/IDSA/PIDS/SIDP vancomycin AUC-guided TDM guideline (target AUC 400–600) — IDSA.
  • International Club of Ascites HRS-AKI criteria & management (albumin challenge, terlipressin) — see CONFIRM below.

Landmark trials

TrialYearTopicResult & why it matters
ELAIN2016RRT timingSingle-center, surgical: early RRT ↓ 90-day mortality (39.3% vs 54.7%, HR 0.66). The lone positive outlier — not generalized.
AKIKI2016RRT timingNo mortality difference; ~49% of the delayed arm never needed RRT. Watchful waiting spares dialysis.
IDEAL-ICU2018RRT timing (septic shock)No 90-day mortality difference; stopped for futility.
STARRT-AKI2020RRT timingn=3,019: no mortality difference; accelerated → more RRT dependence at 90 d (10.4% vs 6.0%) & more adverse events. Practice-defining.
AKIKI 22021RRT timing“More-delayed” no better and trended to harm — no benefit to waiting even longer.
ATN (VA/NIH)2008RRT doseIntensive vs less-intensive RRT: no mortality difference.
RENAL2009RRT doseEffluent 40 vs 25 mL/kg/h: no benefit → dose 20–25 mL/kg/h.
SMART2018FluidsBalanced vs saline (n=15,802): ↓ MAKE30 (14.3% vs 15.4%). Nudged practice toward balanced crystalloids.
SALT-ED2018Fluids (non-ICU)Balanced ↓ MAKE30 in non-critically-ill adults.
BaSICS2021FluidsBalanced vs saline (n=11,052): no 90-day mortality difference.
PLUS2022FluidsPlasma-Lyte vs saline (n=5,037): no difference in mortality or new RRT. Net: balanced safe, avoid large-volume saline.
DOSE2011Diuretics (ADHF)High vs low dose, bolus vs continuous: no primary difference; high-dose gave more diuresis with transient reversible ↑SCr.
PRESERVE2018Contrast-AKI preventionNo benefit of IV bicarbonate over saline, and no benefit of oral NAC. Use isotonic saline only.
CONFIRM2021HRS-AKITerlipressin + albumin ↑ HRS reversal (32% vs 17%) but more respiratory failure; basis for FDA approval of terlipressin.
